title: Graceful Degradation Handover Protocol and Lease QoS — PRD (sketch)
content:
Purpose
This doc sketches a proposal for a graceful-degradation handover protocol that lets Dedicated tenants safely degrade or transfer active capacity when pool pressure, thermal events, or scheduled maintenance threaten SLAs. The goal is predictable tenant behavior (QoS) instead of sudden hard preemptions: minimize tail latency spikes, provide clear telemetry, and enable automated or manual handovers to fallback capacity.

Why this is different / problem statement
- Current behavior on heavy contention: preemptive eviction or hard throttling with inconsistent customer signals and poor troubleshooting context.
- Customers want predictable contracted behavior (commitments) but also need the platform to preserve fleet health and reduce blast radius during incidents.
- We can provide a controlled handover that preserves correctness (no lost requests), keeps latency bounded for critical lanes, and offers a quantifiable contract for fallback.

Key concepts (vocabulary)
- Lease: reserved compute capacity (GPU slots) associated with a tenant commitment.
- QoS lane: latency/throughput class within a tenant (hot, warm, background).
- Handover: coordinated migration of queued/in-flight requests or routing policy change from Dedicated to fallback (hosted/shared) or to degraded local mode.
- Soft-stop: a signaled phase where new requests are slowed/redirected but not forcibly killed.
- Handover token: ephemeral capability that authorizes a fallback target to accept in-flight or prefetched KV caches.

Primary goals
- Predictability: tenants see documented, observable degradation behavior instead of opaque evictions.
- Safety: no silent request loss; all transitions have observable account of affected requests and tokens.
- Controllability: operators and tenants can configure policies (auto-handovers, manual-approve, never-fallback) per lease.
- Economics: fallbacks may incur metered usage/tokens; billing signals communicated at transition.

High-level flow (happy-path autoscaling -> soft degrade -> handover)
1) Autoscaler detects insufficient headroom to maintain QoS targets in the Dedicated pool for next 5m window.
2) Autoscaler signals tenants with at-risk leases (API event + Console notification + per-token metrics flagged).
3) Platform computes a Handover Plan: candidates for partial routing (background lanes first), estimated token delta, and fallback targets (hosted model variants or smaller model/quantized variant in same pool).
4) If tenant policy = auto, orchestrator initiates soft-stop for low-priority QoS lanes (grace window 30–120s). During soft-stop, serving runtime: return 503s with Retry-After for non-critical, continue progress for critical lanes with limited concurrency.
5) For workloads that require continuity, orchestrator issues Handover Tokens to fallback endpoints which can pull prefetched KV cache and resume in-flight sessions.
6) Routing layer updates per-tenant route: some percentage of new requests are routed to fallback; telemetry logs handover token use.
7) After stabilization (pool headroom returns or fallback completes), routes are migrated back according to rollout policy.

Fallback targets (examples)
- Hosted API (Redwood-hosted multitenant): fast path but different SLA and billing.
- Dedicated smaller model (quantized variant) in a neighboring pool: lower cost/latency tradeoff.
- Queueing-with-backpressure: convert bursts into delayed work with progress callbacks.

API/Config surface (sketch)
- Lease QoS policy (per-lease): {auto_handover: boolean, preferred_fallbacks: [hosted, quantized-variant], priority_lanes: ["hot","warm","background"], grace_window_seconds: int, billing_on_handover: enum(tenant_billed, platform_billed, shared_credit)}
- Handover Plan endpoint: GET /tenants/{t}/leases/{l}/handover-plan -> returns node list, estimated delta_tokens_per_minute, route percentage recommendations (stringified JSON returned in API; Console offers UI).
- Handover action endpoint: POST /tenants/{t}/leases/{l}/handover?mode=auto|manual&percent=10..100 -> returns handover-token (opaque string) and expiration.

Runtime guarantees and limits
- Handover-token lifetime: default 90s, configurable up to 5m.
- Maximum percent of hot-lane traffic allowed to fall back without approval: 20% (configurable).
- Prefetch/transfer limitations: Max KV segments transferrable per handover = 50 (protects network).

Observability requirements
- New metrics: handover.initiated, handover.completed, handover.failed, handover.tokens_issued, handover.tokens_consumed, lease.qos_degradation_latency_pct95, fallback.routed_pct.
- Console page: per-lease timeline showing events (autoscale warning, handover start/complete), token ids, affected request ids (sampled), cost delta estimate for month.
- Paging rules: handover.failed alerts SRE and tenant Ops if > X per hour.

Simulation & testing plan
- Build a small simulator (60–90m) that replays realistic tenant traffic patterns with bursts and thermal events. Evaluate: tail latency, percent of requests handed over, KV cache hit delta, and cost delta.
- Chaos tests: simulate node thermal trip (5–10% node loss) and verify handover completes within configured grace windows without request loss for hot lanes.
- Tenant safety validation: create synthetic tenant which sets "never_fallback" and ensure orchestration respects policy (but generate operator escalation path).

Operational playbook (runbook highlights)
- Auto-handover triggered: verify plan in Console -> monitor handover.tokens_consumed -> if failures spike, abort and route to manual degrade.
- Manual takeover: ops can force handover with percent increments (10% steps) to watch latency and cost.
- Post-mortem artifacts: include token ids, time windows, and sampled request ids.

Billing implications (early thinking)
- Default: tenant-billed for fallback compute; platform could offer a grace credit for first 10 minutes per incident for high-tier customers.
- Console shows live cost-accumulator while fallback is active.

Open questions / decisions to make
- How do we securely transfer/validate KV caches cross-pool without exposing tenant secrets? (Need HSM/KMS gating for cache encryption keys)
- Minimum handover-token lifetime that avoids frequent churn but doesn't allow long-lived cross-tenant capabilities?
- What are sensible defaults for percent fallback on hot lanes? 20% vs 10% — run sims.
- Do we support cross-region handovers or restrict to same-region fallbacks? Latency and data residency concerns.

Next steps (short-term)
- Align with serving-runtime on handover-token semantics and KV prefetch packaging (owner: Miguel) — 2 wks
- Prototype Handover Plan endpoint + Console mockups (owner: Lena) — 2 wks
- Simple simulator harness and one-shot chaos test (owner: Rahul) — 3 wks
- Draft operator runbook and updated SLAs for fallbacks (owner: Samir) — 1.5 wks

Notes to self / rough ideas
- Could combine with creditless soft-fence idea: instead of moving traffic, temporarily throttle other opportunistic tenants. That reduces billing complexity but risks fairness.
- Consider exposing a "handover-explain" API that returns why candidate requests were selected for fallback (helps debuggability).

References and related docs (internal)
- capacity-conservator-proposal-autoscale-brokering-wip (design notes)
- graceful-fallback-orchestration-and-token-handoff-prd-draft (older attempt — extract lessons)
- slot-based-burst-scheduler-and-latency-fences-prd-proposal

TODOs (immediate)
- Add example JSON payloads for Handover Plan and POST body (API design session) — TODO (Lena)
- Run sims comparing 10% v 20% hot-lane fallback defaults — TODO (Rahul)
- Security review for token lifecycle and KV transfer encryption — TODO (security)

End of sketch.

(Informal: this is intentionally a sketch — want product + runtime + SRE alignment before turning into a full PRD. Emulating an operator-safe, customer-configurable handover mechanism should make Dedicated more predictable and reduce noisy-eviction support issues.)
